issues.legal_issue: A summary authority under the senior-citizen welfare law may order eviction only when eviction is necessary to protect or maintain a senior citizen and the competing claims in the dispute have been considered.
material_facts: Senior-citizen parents sought the eviction of their daughter-in-law from a home in which she said she had lived with her husband and daughter as a matrimonial residence.
The home had been transferred from the husband to his father and then gifted to his mother amid an ongoing matrimonial dispute.
The daughter-in-law claimed a right to reside in the home, while the senior citizens sought its recovery.
The authorities ordered eviction without adequately addressing the competing residence claim.
issues.conclusion: Although a tribunal may have authority to order eviction when necessary and expedient to secure a senior citizen’s maintenance or protection, it cannot use summary eviction to defeat a competing claim to a shared household without considering that claim. The eviction order was set aside, leaving the residence claim to be determined by the appropriate forum.
issues.legal_principle: The Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007 provides for maintenance and protection of senior citizens, including through Sections 2(b), 3, 4, 7, 8 and 23. The tribunal’s powers may permit eviction when needed to secure maintenance or protection, but the remedy depends on consideration of competing claims. Sections 2(s), 17 and 19 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 provide for a woman’s claim to reside in a shared household and for residence orders; that claim cannot be nullified through summary eviction under the 2007 Act.

predicates.senior_citizen_property_protection_proce: A proceeding is brought to protect the property or maintenance interests of a senior citizen.
predicates.eviction_sought_against_woman_claiming_s: A party seeks to evict a woman who claims that the residence is a home in which she lived in a domestic relationship.
predicates.competing_residence_claims_unassessed: The decision-maker orders eviction without considering the competing claims to reside in the home.

issues.definition: When a senior-citizen property-protection proceeding seeks to evict a woman claiming a shared home and the competing residence claims have not been assessed, summary eviction cannot displace her residence claim.

issues.legal_issue: Competing remedies under welfare laws must be harmonized rather than allowing one law’s overriding clause automatically to extinguish a protected claim under another law.
material_facts: Senior citizens sought eviction through a summary proceeding while the daughter-in-law asserted a residence claim in a home she said she had shared with her husband.
The claimed residence protection arose under a separate law addressing domestic violence, and the senior-citizen proceeding risked preventing her from pursuing that remedy.
The court found that the dispute involved competing claims protected by both laws.
issues.conclusion: The two statutory schemes must be read harmoniously. A tribunal must consider competing claims and mould relief accordingly; the senior-citizen law’s overriding clause cannot be used to defeat the woman’s claim to a shared household.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007 and Section 36 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 must be construed harmoniously. The court relied on Bank of India v. Ketan Parekh and Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India for the approach to competing special statutes and non obstante clauses, and emphasized that statutory interpretation should harmonize rather than excise. The distinct purposes of protecting senior citizens and protecting women from domestic violence must both be given effect.

predicates.dispute_involving_competing_welfare_stat: A dispute involves claims for relief under separate laws enacted to protect vulnerable groups.
predicates.one_remedy_would_extinguish_another_prot: Granting one remedy would prevent a party from pursuing a competing claim protected by another law.

issues.definition: When competing welfare-law claims are in dispute and granting one remedy would extinguish another protected claim, the remedies must be harmonized and both claims considered.

issues.legal_issue: A home may qualify as a shared household even if the woman has no ownership interest in it and it belongs to a relative of her husband.
material_facts: The woman had lived in the home with her husband during their domestic relationship.
The home had been transferred to her husband’s parents, who sought her eviction.
She claimed that the home was her shared household and sought the protection available in relation to such a home.
issues.conclusion: The home could qualify as a shared household despite being owned by the husband’s relatives and despite the woman having no title or interest in it. Whether the premises constituted a shared household had to be determined by the appropriate forum.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(s) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act 2005 defines a shared household through an exhaustive “means and includes” formulation. Read with Sections 17 and 19, it does not require the woman to own or rent the home; it can include a home belonging to a joint family of which the respondent is a member or a home owned by a relative of the husband with whom the woman lived in a domestic relationship. The court relied on Satish Chander Ahuja v. Sneha Ahuja and, on the interpretive effect of “means and includes” definitions, Jagir Singh v. State of Bihar, Kasilingam v. P.S.G. College of Technology, Bharat Coop. Bank (Mumbai) Ltd. v. Coop. Bank Employees Union, and Paul Enterprise v. Rajib Chatterjee and Company.

predicates.domestic_violence_residence_claim: A woman seeks residence protection in a proceeding concerning domestic violence.
predicates.woman_lived_in_home_during_domestic_rela: The woman lived in the home, alone or with the respondent, during a domestic relationship.
predicates.home_owned_by_husbands_relative: The home is owned by a relative of the woman's husband with whom she lived in a domestic relationship.
predicates.home_belongs_to_joint_family_of_responde: The home belongs to a joint family of which the respondent is a member.

issues.definition: If a woman seeks domestic-violence residence protection and lived in the home during a domestic relationship, the home can qualify as a shared household when it is owned by her husband’s relative or belongs to a joint family of which the respondent is a member, regardless of her ownership.

issues.legal_issue: A senior citizen’s right to receive maintenance out of an estate may be enforced against a transferee of that estate who had notice of the right or received the transfer gratuitously.
material_facts: The court considered the scope of the provision governing enforcement of a senior citizen’s pre-existing right to receive maintenance out of an estate when the estate or part of it is transferred.
The court distinguished that provision from the separate provision concerning a transfer made by a senior citizen subject to a condition that the transferee provide maintenance.
issues.conclusion: The maintenance right may be enforced against a transferee with notice of the right or against a gratuitous transferee, and the transfer need not have been made by the senior citizen.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23(2) of the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007 applies where a senior citizen has a right to receive maintenance out of an estate and the estate or part of it is transferred. Unlike Section 23(1), it is not confined to a transfer by the senior citizen. Sections 2(b) and 2(f) support a broad understanding of maintenance and property, including rights or interests in property, and the expression “transfer” is to be read in light of the Act’s beneficial purpose.

rule.if: senior_citizen_estate_maintenance_claim and estate_or_interest_transferred and (transferee_had_notice_of_maintenance_right or transfer_was_gratuitous)

predicates.senior_citizen_estate_maintenance_claim: A senior citizen has a right to receive maintenance out of an estate.
predicates.estate_or_interest_transferred: The estate, part of it, or an interest in it is transferred.
predicates.transferee_had_notice_of_maintenance_rig: The transferee knew of the senior citizen’s right to receive maintenance from the estate.
predicates.transfer_was_gratuitous: The estate or interest was transferred without consideration.

issues.definition: Where a senior citizen has a maintenance claim out of an estate and the estate or an interest in it is transferred, the claim can be enforced against a transferee who had notice of the right or received the transfer gratuitously.
